---
  title: "Research"
---
  
I study population health in data-scarce settings. One side of my work develops childhood sex ratios as a proxy for early-life mortality: because boys die at higher rates in infancy, the sex composition of surviving children carries a mortality signal that a census can recover even when we lack vital statistics. I apply this novel indicator to the historical US, where we lack vital statistics but have excellent census data.

Another strand of my work focuses on maternal-infant health in contemporary sub-Saharan Africa, based on Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data. 

# Publications

<details class="details-example">
    <summary> **Infant Mortality among US Whites in the 19th Century: 
    New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios** 
    with James R. Irwin · <em>Demographic Research</em>. 2025.
    </summary>
    <p>
    Uses childhood sex ratios, which skew female when infant mortality is high, to
    estimate 19th-century US infant mortality. Estimates for US whites are roughly
    70–80 deaths per 1,000 in the mid-1800s.
    </p>
    <p><a href="https://www.demographic-research.org/articles/volume/52/10">Demographic Research</a> 52: 303–350.</p>
</details>

<details class="details-example">
    <summary> **Child Anemia and the 2008 Food Price Crisis in Senegal**  · 
    <em>Demographic Research</em>. 2024.
    </summary>
    <p>
    Examines how the 2008 food price crisis affected child hemoglobin in Senegal,
    using a quasi-experimental comparison of in-utero and breastfeeding children.
    Urban areas, especially Dakar, saw large negative effects, while rural areas
    showed none.
    </p>
    <p><a href="https://www.demographic-research.org/articles/volume/51/20">Demographic Research</a> 51: 637–668.</p>
</details>

# Working Papers

<details class="details-example">
    <summary> **The Hidden Costs of Mass Deportations: 
    Early-Life Mortality and the 1930s Mexican Repatriation** 
    with Sergio Eduardo López Araiza Bejar (October 2026)
    </summary>
    <p>
    The repatriation campaigns of the 1930s removed a large share of the Mexican-origin
    population of the United States, including many US-born children. We use childhood
    sex ratios to estimate the effect on early-life mortality among Mexican immigrants in Texas. 
    We find that the campaign caused a major shift towards females among the affected population, 
    implying a large increase in early life mortality. 
    </p>
    <p><a href="https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.northwestern.edu/dist/c/9329/files/2026/10/sergio_jmp_draft_1015.pdf">Draft</a></p>
</details>

# Works in Progress

- **Black Health in Slavery and Freedom: New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios.**
  With James R. Irwin. Estimates infant mortality among US Black and white populations,
  1850–1880, using childhood sex ratios and European vital statistics.

- **Comparing the JMP Drinking Water Ladder and the HWISE Scale in the 2022–23
  Mozambique DHS.** With Sera Young and Indira Bose. Compares an infrastructure-based
  and an experience-based measure of household water access in a single survey.

- **Solving the Antebellum Puzzle: New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios.**

- **Sex Ratio at Birth and the HIV Epidemic in South Africa.** With Jenny Trinitapoli.
